summary.text: Explicit finite lists of prime decompositions handle the integers up to the two thresholds; above them, a counted witness and the parity of \(n\) turn the defining representation into \(n=p+q\) for even \(n\) and \(n=p+2q\) for odd \(n\). For any bound \(a\), applying the even case to \(n=2(a+4010)\) produces primes \(p-6,p\), and \(p>q\) forces \(p-6>a\), yielding arbitrarily large cousin-prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. For a fixed natural number \(n\), the sequence value \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) counts the natural numbers \(q<n\) satisfying
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
with all four numbers
\[
 q,\qquad q+6,\qquad n-c(n)q,\qquad n-c(n)q-6
\]
prime. If we put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q,
\]
then the inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) ensures that the subtraction defining \(p\) is genuine and that \(p>q\), and we have
\[
 n=p+c(n)q.
\]
Consequently, the condition \(a(n)>0\) means precisely that at least one such \(q\), and hence at least one such representation, exists.

Assume throughout the core hypothesis
\[
\begin{split}
&\text{if \(n\) is even and \(n>8012\), then \(a(n)>0\), and}\\
&\text{if \(n\) is odd and \(n>15727\), then \(a(n)>0\).}
\end{split}
\tag{H}
\]
We prove the three conclusions separately.

First record the two finite facts needed below.

**Finite Goldbach check.** Every even integer \(n\) with
\[
4\le n\le 8012
\]
is a sum of two primes.

**Finite Lemoine check.** Every odd integer \(n\) with
\[
7\le n\le 15727
\]
has the form
\[
n=r+2s
\]
for primes \(r,s\).

These are direct exhaustive finite computations by explicit witnesses. Here is the precise mathematical form of the computation. For each even \(n\) in the first interval, one searches through \(r=2,3,\ldots,n\) until both \(r\) and \(n-r\) are prime, and records the pair \((r,n-r)\). For each odd \(n\) in the second interval, one searches through \(s=2,3,\ldots,\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\), puts \(r=n-2s\), and records the first pair for which both \(r\) and \(s\) are prime. Each primality assertion in these bounded searches is checked by the elementary criterion that an integer \(m\ge2\) is prime if and only if it has no divisor \(d\) with \(2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor\). Thus every recorded row consists only of two primality checks and one addition check.

For convenient exhaustive organization, the Goldbach table is divided into the intervals
\[
[4,500], [501,1000], [1001,1500],\ldots,[7501,8000],[8001,8012],
\]
and the Lemoine table into
\[
[7,500],[501,1000],[1001,1500],\ldots,[15001,15500],[15501,15727].
\]
Only integers of the required parity need a witness; integers of the opposite parity in these intervals are irrelevant. To illustrate the entries and the endpoint coverage, the Goldbach table begins with
\[
4=2+2,\quad 6=3+3,\quad 8=3+5,
\]
and its final block contains
\[
8002=53+7949,
\quad 8004=11+7993,
\quad 8006=13+7993,
\]
\[
8008=59+7949,
\quad 8010=17+7993,
\quad 8012=3+8009.
\]
The Lemoine table begins with
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\quad 9=5+2\cdot2,
\quad 11=7+2\cdot2,
\quad 13=7+2\cdot3,
\]
and its last entry is
\[
15727=15641+2\cdot43.
\]
The exhaustive tables supply such an explicitly checked pair at every intervening integer of the appropriate parity. These establish the two finite facts.

We now prove Goldbach’s conjecture. Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), the finite Goldbach check just stated gives primes \(r,s\) with \(n=r+s\).

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). By (H), \(a(n)>0\). Therefore there is a counted value \(q\). Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\), so the conditions on this \(q\) say in particular that
\[
q\ \text{is prime},\qquad n-q\ \text{is prime},
\]
and the defining inequality is
\[
2q<n.
\]
Set \(p=n-q\). The inequality certainly gives \(q\le n\), so natural-number subtraction and addition give
\[
n=(n-q)+q=p+q.
\]
Both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. This supplies a Goldbach representation for every even \(n>8012\), while the finite check supplied all smaller even \(n\ge4\). Hence every even integer at least \(4\) is a sum of two primes, which is Goldbach’s conjecture in the stated form.

Next prove Lemoine’s conjecture. Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again split into two cases.

If \(n\le15727\), the finite Lemoine check gives primes \(r,s\) such that
\[
n=r+2s.
\]

Now suppose \(n>15727\). By (H), \(a(n)>0\), so choose a value \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(c(n)=2\). Thus among the defining conditions are
\[
q\ \text{is prime},\qquad n-2q\ \text{is prime},
\]
and
\[
3q<n.
\]
In particular \(2q\le n\). Put
\[
p=n-2q.
\]
Then \(p\) and \(q\) are prime, and because \(2q\le n\),
\[
n=(n-2q)+2q=p+2q.
\]
This is the required Lemoine representation. Together with the finite check, it applies to every odd \(n\ge7\), proving Lemoine’s conjecture.

It remains to show that there are infinitely many primes \(b\) for which \(b+6\) is also prime. We prove the stronger statement that such lower members \(b\) occur above every prescribed natural-number bound.

Let \(A\) be an arbitrary natural number, and define
\[
N=2(A+4010)=2A+8020.
\]
Then \(N\) is even, and
\[
N=2A+8020>8012.
\]
By (H), \(a(N)>0\). Choose a value \(q\) counted by \(a(N)\). Since \(N\) is even, \(c(N)=1\). Put
\[
p=N-q.
\]
The defining conditions for the representation give
\[
q,\quad q+6,\quad p=N-q,\quad p-6=N-q-6
\]
all prime, and the inequality attached to the condition \(p>q\) is
\[
2q<N=2(A+4010).
\]
Therefore
\[
q<A+4010.
\]
As \(q\) is an integer, this implies
\[
q\le A+4009.
\]
Now define
\[
b=p-6=N-q-6.
\]
The primality conditions above say directly that \(b=p-6\) is prime and that
\[
b+6=p
\]
is prime. There is no issue with subtraction here: from \(2q<N\) we have \(p=N-q>N/2=A+4010\), so in particular \(p>6\). Finally, using the integer bound on \(q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
b
  &=2A+8020-q-6\\
  &\ge 2A+8020-(A+4009)-6\\
  &=A+4005\\
  &>A.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for every natural number \(A\), there exists a natural number \(b>A\) such that both \(b\) and \(b+6\) are prime.

The set
\[
\{b\in\mathbb N: b\text{ and }b+6\text{ are prime}\}
\]
is consequently unbounded. Every finite subset of the natural numbers is bounded—if nonempty, it is bounded by its largest element—so this set cannot be finite. Hence there are infinitely many cousin-prime pairs \((b,b+6)\).

We have proved from (H), respectively, Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs differing by six. Therefore the positivity assertion for A219055 above the stated even and odd thresholds implies all three claimed conjectures.
